claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2A demonstrating co-localization with TMRE (mitochondria) and nuclear localization.

claims.claim: hoe-1 contains two functional start codons.
claims.source: hoe-1 contains two functional start codons.
claims.evidence: Stated as a fact based on sequence analysis.

claims.claim: Translation beginning from the first start codon (M1) produces a protein containing a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS).
claims.source: Translation beginning from the first start codon (encoding methionine 1 (M1)) produces a protein containing a mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS).
claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis and known protein targeting mechanisms.

claims.claim: Translation beginning from the second start codon (M74) produces a nuclear specific protein.
claims.source: Translation beginning from the second start codon (encoding methionine 74 (M74)), which is 3' to the MTS, produces a nuclear specific protein.
claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis and protein targeting mechanisms.

claims.claim: The feature of two functional start codons is conserved in human ELAC2.
claims.source: This feature is conserved in human ELAC2 and it has been shown that mutating M1 to an alanine produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout (Brzezniak et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claims.claim: Mutating M1 to alanine in human ELAC2 produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout.
claims.source: This feature is conserved in human ELAC2 and it has been shown that mutating M1 to an alanine produces a mitochondrial-specific knockout (Brzezniak et al., 2011).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claims.claim: The hoe-1(ΔMTS) mutation is sufficient to strongly attenuate mitochondrial targeting without impacting nuclear localization.
claims.source: This mutation is sufficient to strongly attenuate mitochondrial targeting without impacting nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals.
claims.source: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 and cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claims.claim: UPRmt reporter activation by cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals.
claims.source: UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 and cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals (Figure 2C and D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claims.claim: UPRmt reporter activation is slightly elevated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals relative to wildtype.
claims.source: In fact, UPRmt reporter activation is slightly elevated in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals relative to wildtype.
claims.evidence: Supported by quantification data in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial HOE-1 is not required for UPRmt activation.
claims.source: These data suggest that mitochondrial HOE-1 is not required for UPRmt activation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals do not show attenuated UPRmt.

claims.claim: HOE-1 is predicted to contain two nuclear localization signals (NLS).
claims.source: HOE-1 is predicted to contain two nuclear localization signals (NLS).
claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis and prediction algorithms.

claims.claim: hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested.
claims.source: Given that hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested and hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype we reasoned that completely ablating nuclear localization of HOE-1 may result in recapitulation of the null phenotype.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from earlier experiments.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype.
claims.source: Given that hoe-1 null mutant animals are developmentally arrested and hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals are superficially wildtype we reasoned that completely ablating nuclear localization of HOE-1 may result in recapitulation of the null phenotype.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from earlier experiments.

claims.claim: The hoe-1(ΔNLS) mutations are sufficient to strongly attenuate, but not completely ablate, HOE-1 nuclear localization whilst still allowing animals to develop to adulthood.
claims.source: These mutations are sufficient to strongly attenuate, but not completely ablate, HOE-1 nuclear localization whilst still allowing animals to develop to adulthood (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C.

claims.claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 robustly attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by spg-7 RNAi.
claims.source: In contrast to loss of mitochondrial HOE-1, loss of nuclear HOE-1 robustly attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by spg-7 RNAi (Figure 2E and F)
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and F.

claims.claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by nuo-6(qm200).
claims.source: and attenuates UPRmt reporter activation induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 2G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G and H.

claims.claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target gene hsp-6 under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Furthermore, loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target genes hsp-6 (Figure 2I) and cyp-14A1.4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2I.

claims.claim: Loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target gene cyp-14A1.4 under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
claims.source: Furthermore, loss of nuclear HOE-1 attenuates the transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target genes hsp-6 (Figure 2I) and cyp-14A1.4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 5A) under conditions of mitochondrial stress.
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5A.

claims.claim: HOE-1 is required in the nucleus to facilitate UPRmt activation.
claims.source: Together these data suggest that HOE-1 is required in the nucleus to facilitate UPRmt activation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from multiple experiments showing that nuclear, but not mitochondrial, HOE-1 is required for UPRmt.

claims.claim: HOE-1 has both nuclear localization signals and a nuclear export signal (NES).
claims.source: Like many nuclear localized proteins (la Cour et al., 2004), HOE-1 has both nuclear localization signals and a nuclear export signal (NES).
claims.evidence: Based on sequence analysis and citation to general knowledge about nuclear proteins.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals are superficially wildtype in their development but are sterile.
claims.source: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals are superficially wildtype in their development but are sterile.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental characterization of the mutant.

claims.claim: Homozygous hoe-1(ΔNES) animals have elevated nuclear HOE-1 accumulation relative to wildtype.
claims.source: Homozygous hoe-1(ΔNES) animals have elevated nuclear HOE-1 accumulation relative to wildtype (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and Figure 2—figure supplement 4B and C.

claims.claim: The UPRmt reporter hsp-6p::GFP is robustly activated in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals similarly to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) and atfs-1(et15) mutant animals.
claims.source: Strikingly, the UPRmt reporter hsp-6p::GFP is robustly activated in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals similarly to that seen in mitochondrial stressor nuo-6(qm200) and constitutive UPRmt activation in atfs-1 gain-of-function (atfs-1(et15)) mutant animals (Figure 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) mildly induces the UPRmt reporter hsp-60p::GFP.
claims.source: hoe-1(ΔNES) also mildly induces the less sensitive UPRmt reporter hsp-60p::GFP (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The UPRmt gene hsp-6 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The UPRmt gene clec-47 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The UPRmt gene cyp-14A4.1 is upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: We found that the UPRmt genes encoding a chaperone protein (hsp-6), stress response involved C-type lectin (clec-47), and P450 enzyme (cyp-14A4.1) are all upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3C, D and E).
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: UPRmt activation is dependent upon the transcription factor ATFS-1.
claims.source: UPRmt activation is dependent upon the transcription factor ATFS-1 (Haynes et al., 2010; Nargund et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3F and G), showing that UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3F and G.

claims.claim: UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
claims.source: Knockdown of atfs-1 is sufficient to completely attenuate UPRmt reporter activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3F and G), showing that UPRmt induction by hoe-1(ΔNES) is ATFS-1 dependent.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that atfs-1 RNAi blocks hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNLS+ΔNES) animals have UPRmt reporter activation comparable to wildtype animals.
claims.source: Indeed, hoe-1(ΔNLS+ΔNES) animals have UPRmt reporter activation comparable to wildtype animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and B.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔMTS+ΔNES) animals have even higher activation of UPRmt than hoe-1(ΔNES) alone.
claims.source: Consistent with our hypothesis, hoe-1(ΔMTS+ΔNES) animals have even higher activation of UPRmt than hoe-1(ΔNES) alone (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4A and B.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) triggers UPRmt activation due to elevated nuclear HOE-1 levels.
claims.source: Taken together, these data strongly suggest that hoe-1(ΔNES) triggers UPRmt activation due to elevated nuclear HOE-1 levels.
claims.evidence: Inferred from experiments showing that nuclear localization is required and that preventing nuclear export is sufficient for UPRmt activation.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals appear to have UPRmt activated specifically in the intestine.
claims.source: Contrary to UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) and atfs-1(et15), hoe-1(ΔNES) animals appear to have UPRmt activated specifically in the intestine (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: UPRmt has been shown to be able to be signaled across tissues, particularly from neurons to intestine.
claims.source: We questioned if this UPRmt activation is occurring cell autonomously or non-cell autonomously as UPRmt has been shown to be able to be signaled across tissues, particularly from neurons to intestine (Durieux et al., 2011; Berendzen et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only attenuated when HOE-1 is selectively degraded in the intestine.
claims.source: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is only attenuated when HOE-1 is selectively degraded in the intestine (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by auxin-inducible degradation experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5A and B.

claims.claim: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 activates UPRmt cell-autonomously in the intestine.
claims.source: This data strongly suggests that compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 activates UPRmt cell-autonomously in the intestine.
claims.evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific degradation experiments.

claims.claim: The UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: We find that the UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3H and I.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
claims.source: We find that the UPRER reporter hsp-4p::GFP is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 3H and I), suggesting that hoe-1(ΔNES) does not cause ER stress nor cellular proteotoxic stress.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of UPRER activation.

claims.claim: The basal reporter ges-1p::GFPcyto is only mildly upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype.
claims.source: Additionally, a basal reporter of GFP that has been used to proxy general protein expression (Gitschlag et al., 2016), ges-1p::GFPcyto, is only mildly upregulated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype (Figure 3J and K).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3J and K.

claims.claim: Impaired nuclear export of HOE-1 specifically activates UPRmt.
claims.source: Together these findings support that impaired nuclear export of HOE-1 specifically activates UPRmt.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the lack of UPRER activation and minimal effect on general protein expression.

claims.claim: UPRmt is known to be triggered when mitochondrial membrane potential is compromised.
claims.source: UPRmt is known to be triggered when mitochondrial membrane potential is compromised (Rolland et al., 2019; Shpilka et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is severely depleted in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: Consistent with UPRmt activation, we found that mitochondrial membrane potential is severely depleted in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation.
claims.source: However, hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals also exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation suggesting that decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4A and B.

claims.claim: Decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction.
claims.source: However, hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals also exhibit compromised mitochondrial membrane potential without UPRmt activation suggesting that decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction (Figure 4A and B).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals have reduced membrane potential but no UPRmt activation.

claims.claim: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi.
claims.source: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi (Figure 4C and D) suggesting that reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
claims.evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claims.claim: Reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
claims.source: Mitochondrial membrane potential is not rescued in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals on atfs-1 RNAi (Figure 4C and D) suggesting that reduced mitochondrial membrane potential in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is not a result of UPRmt activation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking UPRmt does not rescue membrane potential.

claims.claim: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 results in depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.source: Taken together, these data show that compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 results in depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.evidence: Supported by TMRE staining data.

claims.claim: Depletion in membrane potential correlates with UPRmt activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: Furthermore, this depletion in membrane potential correlates with UPRmt activation, consistent with the possibility that hoe-1(ΔNES) activates UPRmt via depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the correlation between reduced membrane potential and UPRmt activation.

claims.claim: UPRmt activation is dependent upon nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor ATFS-1.
claims.source: UPRmt activation is dependent upon nuclear accumulation of the transcription factor ATFS-1 (Nargund et al., 2012; Nargund et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Both hoe-1(ΔNES) and nuo-6(qm200) animals have elevated nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1 relative to wildtype.
claims.source: Both hoe-1(ΔNES) and nuo-6(qm200) animals have elevated nuclear accumulation of ATFS-1 relative to wildtype (Figure 5A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claims.claim: nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype.
claims.source: However, while nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype, hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype.
claims.source: However, while nuo-6(qm200) animals exhibit elevated levels of total cellular and extranuclear levels of ATFS-1::mCherry relative to wildtype, hoe-1(ΔNES) animals do not (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: atfs-1 mRNA levels are elevated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype comparable to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) animals.
claims.source: We find that atfs-1 mRNA levels are also elevated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals relative to wildtype comparable to that seen in nuo-6(qm200) animals (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: Supported by ddPCR data shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: The transcription factor DVE-1 is required for full UPRmt activation.
claims.source: The transcription factor DVE-1 is required for full UPRmt activation (Haynes et al., 2007; Tian et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Accumulation of DVE-1::GFP in intestinal cell nuclei is significantly higher in hoe-1(ΔNES) than in wildtype animals.
claims.source: We found that accumulation of DVE-1::GFP in intestinal cell nuclei is significantly higher in hoe-1(ΔNES) than in wildtype animals (Figure 5E and F).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 5E and F.

claims.claim: UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is a result of increased nuclear accumulation of UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1.
claims.source: Together, these data suggest that UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is a result of increased nuclear accumulation of UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation of increased nuclear levels of both transcription factors.

claims.claim: The canonical role of HOE-1 is to cleave 3'-trailer sequences from nascent tRNAs.
claims.source: The canonical role of HOE-1 is to cleave 3'-trailer sequences from nascent tRNAs (Nashimoto et al., 1999; Mayer et al., 2000; Schiffer et al., 2002; Takaku et al., 2003; Dubrovsky et al., 2004; Brzezniak et al., 2011; Sanchez et al., 2011; Siira et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: The enzymatic function of HOE-1 is dependent upon zinc binding.
claims.source: This enzymatic function is dependent upon zinc binding (Ma et al., 2017; Bienert et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: Animals homozygous for D624A recapitulate the growth arrest phenotype of the hoe-1 null mutant.
claims.source: Animals homozygous for D624A recapitulate the growth arrest phenotype of the hoe-1 null mutant precluding us from assessing the impact of D624A on UPRmt induction in adult hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.evidence: Stated as an observation from experimental characterization of the mutant.

claims.claim: A single copy of catalytically dead hoe-1 is sufficient to attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: A single copy of catalytically dead hoe-1 is sufficient to attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt requires the catalytic activity of HOE-1.
claims.source: These data suggest that hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt requires the catalytic activity of HOE-1.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that a catalytically dead version attenuates UPRmt.

claims.claim: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III.
claims.source: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III followed by sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of tRNA biogenesis.

claims.claim: Mature tRNA production involves sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
claims.source: Production of mature tRNAs begins with transcription of tRNA gene loci by RNA polymerase III followed by sequential cleavage of 5'-leader and 3'-trailer sequences from immature tRNA transcripts by RNase P and HOE-1, respectively.
claims.evidence: Based on established knowledge of tRNA biogenesis.

claims.claim: Following cleavage of 3'-trailer sequences, tRNAs can be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin.
claims.source: Following cleavage of 3'-trailer sequences, tRNAs can be transported to the cytosol by tRNA exportin (Hopper and Nostramo, 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to published study.

claims.claim: rpc-1 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: Indeed, we found that rpc-1 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: rpc-1 RNAi has little impact on mitochondrial stress-induced UPRmt (nuo-6(qm200)).
claims.source: Interestingly, rpc-1 RNAi has little impact on mitochondrial stress-induced UPRmt (nuo-6(qm200)) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C and D.

claims.claim: rpc-1 is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: These data show that rpc-1 is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt and support our hypothesis that increased 3'-tRNA processing by HOE-1 activates UPRmt.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that rpc-1 RNAi blocks hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claims.claim: For the majority of tRNAs 5'-end processing by the RNase P complex is a prerequisite for 3'-end processing by HOE-1.
claims.source: For the majority of tRNAs 5'-end processing by the RNase P complex is a prerequisite for 3'-end processing by HOE-1 (Frendewey et al., 1985; Yoo and Wolin, 1997).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to published studies.

claims.claim: RNAi against popl-1 attenuates UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.source: RNAi against a subunit of the RNase P complex, popl-1, attenuates UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figure 6A and B).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6A and B.

claims.claim: popl-1 RNAi attenuates UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200).
claims.source: popl-1 RNAi also attenuates both UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 6C and D) as well as basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto (Figure 6E and F), albeit to a lesser extent than the attenuation seen in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6C and D.

claims.claim: popl-1 RNAi attenuates basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto.
claims.source: popl-1 RNAi also attenuates both UPRmt induced by nuo-6(qm200) (Figure 6C and D) as well as basal induction of ges-1p::GFPcyto (Figure 6E and F), albeit to a lesser extent than the attenuation seen in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: Elevated 3'-tRNA processing in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is responsible for UPRmt activation.
claims.source: These data suggest that popl-1 RNAi may have a broad impact on protein expression but supports that elevated 3'-tRNA processing in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is responsible for UPRmt activation given that popl-1 RNAi strongly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking 5'-end processing attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claims.claim: xpo-3 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: Strikingly, xpo-3 RNAi robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt(Figure 6G and H).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6G and H.

claims.claim: xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt.
claims.source: However, xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt (Figure 6I and J) nor basal ges-1p::GFP levels (Figure 6K and L).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6I and J.

claims.claim: xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate basal ges-1p::GFP levels.
claims.source: However, xpo-3 RNAi does not attenuate nuo-6(qm200) induced UPRmt (Figure 6I and J) nor basal ges-1p::GFP levels (Figure 6K and L).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6K and L.

claims.claim: In hoe-1(ΔNES) animals 3'-processed tRNAs are required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
claims.source: These data suggest that in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals 3'-processed tRNAs are required in the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that blocking tRNA export attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.

claims.claim: Knockdown of rtcb-1 mildly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: Knockdown of both tRNA ligase, rtcb-1, and tRNA nucleotidyl transferase, hpo-31 mildly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-C.

claims.claim: Knockdown of hpo-31 mildly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: Knockdown of both tRNA ligase, rtcb-1, and tRNA nucleotidyl transferase, hpo-31 mildly attenuate hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: Supported by fluorescence imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-C.

claims.claim: rtcb-1 RNAi mildly attenuates nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt.
claims.source: However, rtcb-1 RNAi also mildly attenuates nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 3D and E).

results.result: HOE-1 is generally required for maximal UPRmt activation, as demonstrated by attenuation of UPRmt reporter (hsp-6p::GFP) induction in hoe-1 RNAi, hoe-1 null, and various mitochondrial stress conditions (nuo-6(qm200), spg-7 RNAi, cco-1 RNAi).
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by multiple independent experimental approaches including RNAi knockdown, null mutants, and different mitochondrial stressors. The data show consistent attenuation of UPRmt across different conditions with appropriate statistical analysis (Figures 1A-G). The use of both genetic null and RNAi provides robust validation.

results.result: HOE-1 localizes to both mitochondria and nuclei in C. elegans, and GFP-tagging does not compromise its essential functions as demonstrated by normal development of tagged animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C12 are supported by confocal imaging showing co-localization with TMRE (mitochondria) and nuclear localization (Figure 2A), complemented by functional validation showing normal development of GFP-tagged animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A). The dual localization is consistent with predictions and ortholog data from other species (C8).

results.result: Mitochondrial HOE-1 is not required for UPRmt activation. The hoe-1(ΔMTS) mutation eliminates mitochondrial targeting without affecting nuclear localization, and UPRmt reporter activation by spg-7 and cco-1 RNAi is not attenuated in these animals.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C22 are well-supported by the ΔMTS mutant analysis. The mutation strategy is based on established principles from human ELAC2 (C16-C17), and imaging confirms loss of mitochondrial localization while preserving nuclear localization (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A). The lack of UPRmt attenuation in hoe-1(ΔMTS) animals (Figures 2C-D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A-B) provides strong evidence that mitochondrial HOE-1 is dispensable for UPRmt.

results.result: Nuclear HOE-1 is required for UPRmt activation. The hoe-1(ΔNLS) mutation attenuates nuclear localization and robustly reduces UPRmt reporter activation induced by spg-7 RNAi and nuo-6(qm200), as well as transcriptional upregulation of UPRmt target genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C31 are strongly supported by the ΔNLS mutant analysis. The mutation attenuates but does not completely ablate nuclear localization while allowing development to adulthood (C26, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A-C). UPRmt attenuation is demonstrated by both reporter fluorescence (Figures 2E-H) and mRNA quantification of target genes (Figure 2I, Figure 2—figure supplement 5A). This provides compelling evidence for nuclear HOE-1's requirement.

results.result: Compromising HOE-1 nuclear export by mutating the NES is sufficient to robustly activate UPRmt in an ATFS-1-dependent manner, with upregulation of multiple UPRmt target genes (hsp-6, clec-47, cyp-14A4.1).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C42 are well-supported by the hoe-1(ΔNES) mutant analysis. The mutation increases nuclear HOE-1 accumulation (C34, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) and robustly activates UPRmt reporters (Figures 3A-B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-B). Multiple UPRmt genes are upregulated (Figures 3C-E), and atfs-1 RNAi completely blocks this activation (Figures 3F-G), demonstrating ATFS-1 dependence. The data are internally consistent and statistically significant.

results.result: UPRmt activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals is due to elevated nuclear HOE-1 levels, as demonstrated by the observation that combining ΔNLS with ΔNES abolishes UPRmt activation, while combining ΔMTS with ΔNES enhances it.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C45 are supported by elegant genetic epistasis experiments. The hoe-1(ΔNLS+ΔNES) double mutant shows wildtype-level UPRmt (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A-B), while hoe-1(ΔMTS+ΔNES) shows enhanced UPRmt (Figure 3—figure supplement 4A-B). This logic strongly supports the conclusion that nuclear HOE-1 levels drive UPRmt activation in the ΔNES background.

results.result: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 activates UPRmt cell-autonomously in the intestine, as demonstrated by tissue-specific degradation experiments using the auxin-inducible degradation system.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 are supported by tissue-specific degradation experiments (Figure 3—figure supplement 5A-B). UPRmt is only attenuated when HOE-1 is degraded in the intestine (ges-1p::TIR1) but not in neurons (rgef-1p::TIR1). However, the degron-tagged allele shows modestly diminished UPRmt activation compared to untagged ΔNES (noted in figure legend), which could affect interpretation. The conclusion of cell-autonomous intestinal activation is reasonable but should be interpreted with this caveat.

results.result: Impaired nuclear export of HOE-1 specifically activates UPRmt without causing ER stress or general proteotoxic stress, as demonstrated by lack of UPRER reporter activation and minimal upregulation of a basal protein expression reporter.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C53 are supported by appropriate control experiments. The UPRER reporter (hsp-4p::GFP) is not activated in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figures 3H-I), and the basal reporter ges-1p::GFPcyto shows only mild upregulation (Figures 3J-K). These controls effectively rule out general proteotoxic stress and support the specificity of UPRmt activation.

results.result: Compromised nuclear export of HOE-1 results in depletion of mitochondrial membrane potential, which correlates with UPRmt activation. However, decreased membrane potential does not guarantee UPRmt induction, and the membrane potential depletion is not a consequence of UPRmt activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C61 are supported by TMRE staining experiments (Figures 4A-D). The hoe-1(ΔNES) animals show severely depleted membrane potential (C55), while hoe-1(ΔNLS) animals show compromised potential without UPRmt activation (C56-C57), demonstrating that membrane potential loss is insufficient for UPRmt. The observation that atfs-1 RNAi does not rescue membrane potential in ΔNES animals (C58-C59) supports that membrane potential loss is upstream of UPRmt. The data are internally consistent.

results.result: UPRmt induction in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals results from increased nuclear accumulation of UPRmt transcription factors ATFS-1 and DVE-1, with elevated nuclear ATFS-1 and DVE-1::GFP levels and increased atfs-1 mRNA.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C69 are well-supported by confocal imaging and molecular data. Both hoe-1(ΔNES) and nuo-6(qm200) show elevated nuclear ATFS-1 (Figures 5A-B), though with different patterns of total cellular ATFS-1 (C64-C65, Figure 5C). The atfs-1 mRNA is elevated in both conditions (Figure 5D), and DVE-1::GFP nuclear accumulation is significantly higher in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals (Figures 5E-F). The data support increased nuclear accumulation of both transcription factors.

results.result: UPRmt activation by hoe-1(ΔNES) requires the catalytic activity of HOE-1, as demonstrated by attenuation of UPRmt in trans-heterozygous animals carrying one copy of catalytically dead hoe-1(D624A).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C74 are supported by the catalytic mutant analysis. The D624A mutation targets a zinc-binding residue essential for enzymatic activity (C71), and homozygous mutants recapitulate the null phenotype (C72). The trans-heterozygous experiment (hoe-1(ΔNES)/hoe-1(D624A+ΔNES)) shows attenuated UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-B), supporting the requirement for catalytic activity. However, the use of trans-heterozygotes rather than homozygotes is a limitation imposed by lethality.

results.result: RNA polymerase III (rpc-1) is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt but has little impact on mitochondrial stress-induced UPRmt, supporting the hypothesis that increased tRNA transcription contributes to HOE-1-mediated UPRmt activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C75-C80 are supported by RNAi experiments showing that rpc-1 knockdown robustly attenuates hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B) but has minimal effect on nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C-D). This differential effect supports the tRNA processing hypothesis. However, rpc-1 knockdown affects all RNA pol III transcripts, not just tRNAs, which limits mechanistic specificity.

results.result: RNase P (popl-1) is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt, supporting that elevated 3'-tRNA processing is responsible for UPRmt activation. However, popl-1 RNAi also attenuates nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt and basal protein expression.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C85 are supported by popl-1 RNAi experiments (Figures 6A-F). The attenuation of hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt is stronger than effects on nuo-6(qm200) or basal expression, supporting the tRNA processing hypothesis. However, the broader effects of popl-1 RNAi (C83-C84) suggest potential pleiotropic effects on protein expression, which somewhat complicates interpretation. The conclusion remains reasonable given the differential magnitude of effects.

results.result: tRNA exportin (xpo-3) is required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt but not for nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt or basal protein expression, suggesting that 3'-processed tRNAs must reach the cytosol to activate UPRmt.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C89 are strongly supported by xpo-3 RNAi experiments (Figures 6G-L). The robust attenuation of hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt without effects on nuo-6(qm200) or basal expression provides compelling evidence that cytosolic tRNAs are required specifically for HOE-1-mediated UPRmt activation. This is one of the most specific and informative results in the manuscript.

results.result: tRNA ligation (rtcb-1) and CCA addition (hpo-31) have limited involvement in hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt, as their knockdown produces only mild attenuation.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C93 are supported by RNAi experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A-E). Both rtcb-1 and hpo-31 knockdown show mild effects on hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt, and rtcb-1 also mildly affects nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt. The conclusion of limited involvement is reasonable, though the mild effects could reflect incomplete knockdown or redundant pathways.

results.result: UPRmt induction by nuclear export-deficient HOE-1 results from increased 3'-tRNA processing, and these tRNA species are required in the cytosol to trigger UPRmt.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C95 synthesize multiple lines of evidence including requirements for catalytic activity (C73-C74), RNA pol III (C78-C80), RNase P (C82-C85), and tRNA export (C86-C89). The convergent evidence from these independent approaches strongly supports the conclusion that increased 3'-tRNA processing and cytosolic tRNA accumulation drive UPRmt activation in hoe-1(ΔNES) animals.

results.result: The integrated stress response (ISR) via GCN2 and eIF2α is not required for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt activation, as demonstrated by only slight reduction of UPRmt in gcn-2 null and eIF2α non-phosphorylatable mutant backgrounds.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C103 are supported by genetic experiments (Figures 7A-B). The minimal effects of gcn-2 deletion or eIF2α mutation on hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt effectively rule out ISR as the primary mechanism. This is an important negative result that helps define the mechanism. The slight reduction observed could reflect minor ISR contribution or indirect effects.

results.result: There is a single hoe-1 transcript in C. elegans, and hoe-1 mRNA levels are modestly elevated in nuo-6(qm200) animals, suggesting transcriptional upregulation under mitochondrial stress.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C107 are supported by ddPCR experiments using two primer pairs (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-C). The similar mRNA levels detected by both primer pairs support a single transcript model (C104-C105), and the modest elevation in nuo-6(qm200) animals suggests transcriptional upregulation (C106-C107). The data are straightforward and well-controlled.

results.result: Nuclear HOE-1 levels are markedly diminished under mitochondrial stress, but this is UPRmt-dependent. When UPRmt is blocked by atfs-1 RNAi, nuclear HOE-1 levels are elevated above wildtype, suggesting that HOE-1 is upregulated upon mitochondrial stress but then negatively regulated by ATFS-1 once UPRmt is activated.
results.evaluation: Claims C108-C113 are supported by confocal imaging and western blot data (Figures 8A-D, Figure 8—figure supplement 2-3). The key observation is that nuclear HOE-1 is reduced under stress (C108) but elevated when atfs-1 is knocked down (C109), with increased total cellular HOE-1 in the atfs-1 RNAi background (C110). This supports a model of stress-induced upregulation followed by ATFS-1-dependent negative regulation. The data are internally consistent and well-controlled.

results.result: UPRmt activation negatively regulates nuclear HOE-1, as demonstrated by markedly reduced nuclear HOE-1 levels in atfs-1(et15) gain-of-function animals with constitutive UPRmt activation, while total and mitochondrial HOE-1 levels remain largely unperturbed.
results.evaluation: Claims C114-C116 are supported by analysis of atfs-1(et15) animals (Figures 8E-H, Figure 8—figure supplement 4). The selective reduction of nuclear HOE-1 without changes in total or mitochondrial HOE-1 provides strong evidence for UPRmt-dependent negative regulation of nuclear HOE-1. This complements the atfs-1 RNAi experiments and supports a feedback mechanism.

results.result: Nuclear HOE-1 is required for maximal UPRmt activation, with varied attenuation depending on how UPRmt is activated. UPRmt induction by RNAi (cco-1 and spg-7) is robustly attenuated by loss of hoe-1, while nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt is only modestly attenuated.
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C128 synthesize earlier findings and are supported by the collective data from Figures 1-2. The differential effects on RNAi-induced versus nuo-6(qm200)-induced UPRmt are consistently observed across multiple experiments. The authors provide a reasonable explanation based on cell-autonomous versus non-cell-autonomous UPRmt activation (C129-C133), though this remains somewhat speculative.

results.result: The differential requirement for hoe-1 in UPRmt activation may reflect that cell-autonomous intestinal UPRmt (induced by RNAi) is hoe-1-dependent, while neuron-to-intestine UPRmt induction (potentially contributing to nuo-6(qm200) effects) may work primarily in a hoe-1-independent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C129-C133 present a speculative model to explain differential hoe-1 requirements. While the premises about RNAi tissue specificity (C129) and non-cell-autonomous UPRmt (C130) are well-established, the specific hypothesis about hoe-1-dependent versus independent pathways (C131-C132) lacks direct experimental support. The tissue-specific degradation experiments (C133) support intestinal cell-autonomous action of HOE-1 but don't directly test the neuron-to-intestine hypothesis. This remains an interesting but unproven model.

results.result: UPRmt activation via hoe-1(ΔNES) correlates with decreased mitochondrial membrane potential and increased nuclear localization of ATFS-1 and DVE-1, consistent with the canonical UPRmt activation mechanism.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C136 are supported by TMRE staining (Figures 4A-B) and transcription factor localization data (Figures 5A-F). The correlation between membrane potential loss and UPRmt activation, along with increased nuclear ATFS-1 and DVE-1, is consistent with established UPRmt mechanisms. However, correlation does not prove causation, and the exact relationship between tRNA processing and membrane potential loss remains unclear.

results.result: Increased 3'-tRNA processing by HOE-1 is responsible for UPRmt activation, as demonstrated by attenuation of hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt when tRNA processing or export is blocked. This represents the first reported connection between altered tRNA processing and UPRmt in C. elegans.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C141 are strongly supported by convergent evidence from multiple experiments (rpc-1, popl-1, xpo-3 RNAi; catalytic mutant). The requirement for tRNA transcription, processing, and export specifically for hoe-1(ΔNES)-induced UPRmt provides compelling mechanistic evidence. The novelty claim (C141) appears justified based on the literature cited. This is a key finding of the manuscript.

results.result: The mechanism by which tRNAs activate UPRmt is independent of the integrated stress response (ISR), likely because increased 3'-end processing results in excess charged tRNAs rather than uncharged tRNAs required for ISR activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C142-C146 are supported by the gcn-2 and eIF2α experiments (Figure 7) and represent reasonable mechanistic interpretation. The lack of ISR involvement (C144) is experimentally demonstrated, and the explanation based on charged versus uncharged tRNAs (C145-C146) is logical, though the actual tRNA charging status is not directly measured. The reasoning is sound but the specific mechanism remains inferential.

results.result: Multiple speculative mechanisms are proposed for how altered tRNA processing might activate UPRmt, including amino acid depletion affecting mitochondrial translation, excessive nuclear-encoded mitochondrial protein translation, selective tRNA upregulation, or involvement of tRNA-like RNAs or fragments.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C155 present multiple speculative mechanisms without direct experimental support. While each hypothesis is plausible and grounded in established biology (C149, C152, C155), none are directly tested. These represent reasonable directions for future investigation but should not be considered established results. The authors appropriately present these as possibilities rather than conclusions.

results.result: Nuclear HOE-1 is dynamically regulated by mitochondrial stress through a feedback mechanism: stress elevates nuclear HOE-1 levels, which increases tRNA processing and triggers UPRmt via ATFS-1 and DVE-1, and activated UPRmt then negatively regulates nuclear HOE-1 levels.
results.evaluation: Claims C156-C161 synthesize the major findings into a coherent model supported by multiple lines of evidence: stress-induced HOE-1 upregulation (C106-C107, C156-C158), HOE-1-dependent UPRmt activation (C159), and ATFS-1-dependent negative regulation (C109-C116, C160-C161). The model is well-supported by the data, though some mechanistic details remain to be elucidated. This represents the central conclusion of the manuscript.

results.result: The findings have potential implications for understanding human diseases associated with ELAC2 mutations (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and prostate cancer), suggesting that altered tRNA processing may trigger aberrant stress response signaling rather than simply causing loss of mature tRNA production.
results.evaluation: Claims C162-C167 discuss translational implications. While ELAC2 mutations are indeed associated with human diseases (C163-C164), and the traditional hypothesis focuses on loss of tRNA production (C165), the alternative mechanism proposed here (C166) is speculative. The C. elegans system may provide a useful model (C167), but direct evidence linking the proposed mechanism to human disease pathology is lacking. These claims represent interesting speculation rather than established results.

results.result: The findings provide a novel mechanism involving the tRNA processing enzyme HOE-1 by which mitochondrial stress is transduced to activate UPRmt, providing important insight into mitochondrial stress response regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C168-C169 represent the overall conclusions of the manuscript and are well-supported by the collective evidence. The work establishes HOE-1 as a novel regulator of UPRmt, demonstrates the requirement for nuclear HOE-1 and tRNA processing/export, and reveals a feedback regulatory mechanism. The novelty and significance of these findings are appropriately stated.
